position_in_era.historical_role: Inversion via harmonic register: Cornell's G–E–Eb–Bb–Ab–C chord progression is built on major-key lush harmony delivered against the weight-first expectation — a sunny, psychedelic melodic riff that uses the same Sabbath-descended slow tempo and heavy distortion but refuses the minor-key darkness. The aesthetic inversion is tonal: Sabbath uses detuning to generate dread; Soundgarden uses detuning (dropped D) to generate surreal beauty. Kim Thayil's guitar is as heavy as Iommi's but the emotional destination is lysergic sunshine, not doom.

narrative_slots.production_facts: Recorded 1993–1994 at London Bridge Studio and Bad Animals Studio, Seattle, produced by Michael Beinhorn. Chris Cornell wrote the song in 15 minutes. Kim Thayil's guitar riff uses a G–E–Eb–Bb–Ab progression in drop D tuning — the detuning is Sabbath-inherited but the chord quality is major/dominant rather than minor/tritone. The slow tempo (73 bpm) matches Sabbath's funeral pace but the sonic atmosphere is dreamlike rather than threatening.
narrative_slots.member_dynamics: Cornell (vocal, riff conception) and Thayil (guitar execution) are the compositional pair. Matt Cameron's drums adapt Sabbath's slow lockstep to a swing feel. Cornell's vocal melody soars above the heavy guitar in a falsetto range — the voice deliberately escapes the weight rather than fighting within it.
narrative_slots.instrumentation_details: Thayil: Gibson SG through a Marshall (like Iommi) in drop D; Cornell: vocal (falsetto range); Cameron: drums; Ben Shepherd: bass. The riff's major-key quality over heavy distortion was unusual in 1994 — the combination of sonic weight and harmonic openness is the inversion's mechanism.
narrative_slots.cultural_venue: Reached #1 US Modern Rock, #2 US Mainstream Rock. Grammys: Best Hard Rock Performance 1995. The music video (directed by Howard Greenhalgh) created a dreamlike image world that visualised the tonal inversion: bright, melting, surreal rather than dark and threatening. One of the most-played songs of 1994.
narrative_slots.release_circumstances: Superunknown released March 1994. The album debuted at #1 US — the first grunge album (after Nevermind) to demonstrate the commercial viability of heavy-but-inverted aesthetics. Cornell's death (2017) has since given the song a posthumous weight it did not originally carry.
